sentence: Apps send AI requests through the router by naming a model group.
Several provider setups, called deployments, can serve one model group.
When a request fails with an error worth retrying and retries are allowed, this part tries the same group again, sometimes after a short wait.
If that does not work, it can send the request to a backup group that the operator listed.
It also counts successes and failures per deployment, and it can bench a failing deployment for a few seconds.
When this part goes wrong, customers wait through extra pauses, get errors a backup could have served, or get nothing back from some features.
An async routed call usually enters the fallback entry, `async_function_with_fallbacks`, which runs the retry loop and hands any final error to the fallback dispatcher.
The loop retries the same model group up to the retry count, while the eligibility check or a retry policy allows it.
For most errors, a group with two or more order levels walks its higher levels and then its fallback chain, returning that walk's result or last error.
Otherwise the dispatcher tries weighted failover if enabled and the group uses simple-shuffle, except on too-long prompts and blocked content.
note: RDISP-106: the dispatcher tries weighted failover "When `enable_weighted_failover` is true, the error is not context-window or content-policy, and no order walk returned"; RDISP-120 adds that it does nothing "unless the group's routing strategy is `simple-shuffle`". The sentence now carries the context-window/content-policy exclusion and the simple-shuffle condition. RDISP-120's further need for a `failed_deployment_id` is left out, but "tries" is RDISP-106's own word for the call, and the dispatcher section states the full condition.

sentence: Then it walks one fallback chain, raising the original error when nothing answers.
note: RDISP-111 gives the generic chain; RDISP-115: "Every path that reaches the end raises the original exception, never a fallback's error." The dispatcher walks at most one of the non-standard, dedicated or generic chains (RDISP-107/RDISP-108/RDISP-111).

sentence: Callbacks count usage and ask for cooldowns, and `factory_function` builds most non-chat endpoints.
model group: the model name a request asks for; one group can hold several deployments.
note: RDISP-042 (`model_group` is "the request's `model`") and RDISP-092 (`original_model_group = <model>`) support the requested name; RDISP-058, now cited, "fetches every healthy deployment of the group", so a group can hold several. The unsupported word "public" is gone.

sentence: deployment: one configured provider setup inside a model group, with its own settings and id.
backup group: another model group the operator lists to try when this one fails.
cooldown: a short pause during which the router sends a deployment no traffic, also called benching; its length is the cooldown time.
fallback entry: the outer step that runs the retry loop and passes a final error to the dispatcher; on a top-level call it first resets the fallback stamps.
retry loop: the part that calls the same model group again after a failure.
retry count: how many extra attempts the loop may make after the first one.
retry policy: an operator's table of retry counts per error type; when it gives a count, that count replaces the retry count and the eligibility check.
eligibility check: the ordered tests that decide whether an error deserves another attempt.
fallback dispatcher: the part that takes the final error and decides where else to send the request.
fallback chain: the ordered list of backup groups tried for a group; a catch-all entry covers groups without their own.
order level: a priority tier among one group's deployments.
weighted failover: an opt-in extra try on the same group's other deployments, for weighted shuffle routing only.
endpoint factory: the builder that wraps a library function as a router endpoint; the endpoint's call type, the kind of operation, decides how it runs and routes.
note: RDISP-001: `factory_function` "only builds and returns a wrapper around `original_function`"; SYS-004, now cited: "their sync or async shape and routing are decided by call type".

sentence: provider and client arguments: an optional provider name and a ready-made connection that a caller can pass.
guardrail block: an error a safety check raises on purpose; the router passes it to the caller with no retry or backup.
too-long prompts: errors saying the request does not fit the model's context window.
blocked content: errors saying the provider refused the request under its content policy.
backoff: the wait before the next attempt, shaped by a header, a floor, a cap and random jitter.
skip list: deployments that refused this request with a non-retryable status, avoided on later retries.
unsupported-parameter switch: whether unsupported-parameter errors and provider 400 errors other than too-long prompts and blocked content may fall back.
note: Matches RDISP-101: "`fallback_on_unsupported_params` is false and the error is an `UnsupportedParamsError`, or a 400 `BadRequestError` with a non-empty `llm_provider` that is neither a context-window nor a content-policy error" (code `is_bad_request_without_fallback` agrees). The context-window/content-policy exclusion is restored.

sentence: lookup groups: the group names the dispatcher looks up in the backup lists: a pre-picked tier, the routed group, the requested group, then the original group.
attempt headers: response headers that report how many retries and fallback hops a reply took.
outcome text: the explanation of what fallback did that the dispatcher appends to the final error's message, while debug exposure is on and outside a nested hop.
success callback: the logging step after each successful provider call that counts the deployment's successes and usage.
failure callback: the logging step after each failed provider call that counts the failure and asks whether to cool the deployment down.
deployment id: a deployment's stable id; when none is configured, the router hashes one from the group name and the settings.
file and batch entries: hand-written endpoints for uploads and batch jobs that skip the factory.
When a call succeeds on its first attempt, `x-litellm-attempted-retries` and `x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks` are 0.
When no retry policy applies, the status is 408, 409, 429 or 500 and above, and a healthy deployment and a retry remain, the loop retries, at once unless the group has exactly one deployment.
When the error is 400, 404 or 422 and no retry policy applies, there is no retry; the dispatcher runs next.
When a retry policy has a count for the error and the request did not set `num_retries` to 0, that count becomes the retry count and bypasses the eligibility check, so even a 400 retries.

When `fallbacks` is unset, no order walk ran, weighted failover returned no reply, and no dedicated list applies, the result is the original error, with outcome text saying no fallback was attempted when exposure is on.
note: RDISP-116: when no order walk or weighted failover returned a response, "`fallbacks` is `None`, and no context-window or content-policy chain applies ... The original exception is raised with the ` No fallback was attempted.` outcome text when exposure is on." "No order walk ran" is the right condition, since a walk that runs returns or raises its last error (RDISP-104, RDISP-105), and "applies" replaces "answered".

sentence: When `fallbacks` is set but has no entry for any of the lookup groups and no catch-all, the result is the original error; with exposure on, outside a nested hop, for an error with a message, a note that no backup group was found replaces the outcome text.
When a failure callback sees a deployment id and no skip case, it adds 1 to `<id>:fails` and asks for a cooldown, 5 s by default.
Most endpoints other than chat come from a builder when the router starts.
Depending on the endpoint's call type, a call then retries and falls back like chat, makes one call to one deployment, or skips the router and calls the provider directly.
Some names match no route and hand the caller an empty result with no error.
Synchronous wrappers cover the main list, such as "responses" and "ocr", plus vector-store, vector-store-file and managed-agent calls.
The main one makes one call to one deployment, with no retries, fallbacks or alert, and silently drops a caller's `custom_llm_provider` and `client`.
Every other call type gets an asynchronous wrapper that runs its first matching branch, and most branches end in the generic async fallback chain.
Some families skip routing instead:
vector-store and interactions calls without a model, and container calls with neither a model nor a routable container id, call the provider directly;
synchronous vector-store-file calls, managed agents and assistants always call the provider directly.
Of the bound names that match no branch, the synchronous-looking ones hand back an un-awaited coroutine.
After a failed attempt, the router decides whether to try the same group again and how often.
An operator's retry policy can set that count per error type; otherwise a few checks rule out errors another try will not fix.
The retry count comes from the request's `num_retries`, then the failing deployment, then the router, then 0.
After the first failure, the loop consults a retry policy when one exists and the request did not set `num_retries` to 0.
Its count replaces the retry count and turns off the eligibility check for the whole request.
Without such a count, the eligibility check re-raises the error at the first test that holds:
a context-window or content-policy error while that error's own fallback list is set;
a non-retryable status other than 401 and 403, where only 408, 409, 429 and 500 or above are retryable;
a not-found error;
a rate-limit error with no healthy deployment left while generic fallbacks exist;
a 401 or 403 in a group with at most 1 deployment;
no healthy deployment left at all.
A count of 0 re-raises the first error unchanged.
A request that names one specific deployment, such as by its id, sees no healthy deployments here, so without a policy it never retries.
Step first (First attempt): The loop calls the group once, and a success returns with zero retries recorded; a guardrail block skips retries entirely.
Step policy (A policy can override): A configured policy count replaces the retry count and skips the check, unless the request set its own retry count to zero.

Step gate (The eligibility check): Without a policy, retries stop on a status not worth retrying, a not-found error, a too-long prompt or blocked content with its own backup list, or no healthy deployment left. A sign-in or permission refusal stops them only in a group with one deployment.
Step wait (The wait): The wait is zero when the group has several deployments and a healthy one remains.
Step left>dispatch (Out of retries): The loop raises the latest error, and the fallback dispatcher takes over.
Between tries the router waits only when the group has a single deployment or no healthy one left.
That pause grows with each try, unless the provider says how long to wait.
Later tries also avoid deployments that rejected the request outright.
When the backoff is not 0 s, a `retry-after` value of 1 to 60 whole seconds wins.
Failing that, the delay starts at 0.5 s by default, doubles per retry used, rises to the router's `retry_after` floor, and caps at 8.0 s.
Either way it adds random jitter, below 0.75 s by default.
note: RDISP-162: "`jitter` is `JITTER * random()`, a value in [0, `JITTER`) with default `JITTER` 0.75 s", added on both the `retry-after` and the exponential path. "By default" now marks 0.75 s as the default.

sentence: When the loop runs to the end, it also sleeps after the final failed retry, then raises the latest error, not the first.
A non-retryable status, such as 400, 401, 403 or 404, puts the failed deployment on the skip list.
Later retries avoid it unless that would leave no candidate, in which case the whole candidate list returns.
In the example, group a's one deployment always answers 500, a server error, the router sets 3 retries, and a falls back to b, without jitter.
With default settings that lone deployment does not cool down after a few failures.
At 0s, group a's one deployment: first call: server error 500; waits 0.5 s.
At 0.5s, group a's one deployment: retry 1: server error 500; waits 1.0 s.
At 1.5s, group a's one deployment: retry 2: server error 500; waits 2 s.
At 3.5s, group a's one deployment: retry 3: server error 500; waits 4.0 s anyway.
At 7.5s, backup group b: dispatcher sends the request here; serves the reply.
At 7.5s, the caller: gets group b's reply; one fallback hop recorded.
When the retry loop gives up, the dispatcher looks for somewhere else to send the request.
For most errors, a group with two or more priority tiers walks its higher tiers, then its backup list, and stops there.
Otherwise one backup list follows an opt-in extra try on the group's other deployments, which too-long prompts and blocked content skip.
note: RDISP-106 runs the opt-in weighted failover only when "the error is not context-window or content-policy, and no order walk returned", and the sentence now says those errors skip it; then one chain follows (RDISP-111, RDISP-108/RDISP-110). The paragraph's later sentence states the simple-shuffle and failed-deployment conditions.

sentence: The dispatcher re-raises unchanged when fallbacks are disabled, no model group is named, or a guardrail intervened.
With `fallback_on_unsupported_params` off, an unsupported-parameter error or a provider 400 that is not context-window or content-policy also stops here.
The order walk needs two or more distinct `order` values and an error that is not context-window or content-policy.
A failed walk raises its last error, with no outcome text.

Weighted failover runs next, only when `enable_weighted_failover` is on, the group uses simple-shuffle, no order walk returned, and the error names the failed deployment and is not context-window or content-policy.
It retries the group without the failed and cooled-down deployments; provider errors and router rate-limit errors from it fall through to the chains, other errors reach the caller.
Then the dispatcher picks one chain:
it walks a non-standard `fallbacks` value, such as a list of model names, as given;
a context-window or content-policy error whose own list is set uses that list alone, and a miss raises the original error;
with that list unset, the error goes on to the generic chain;
the generic chain is the specific entry of the first of the lookup groups that has one, else the `"*"` catch-all entry.
A walk tries targets one at a time, skips those already tried, stops at the depth limit, and marks a successful hop's reply with `x-litellm-attempted-fallbacks` set to its depth.
When `fallbacks` is set but no chain resolves, the dispatcher raises the original error with, when exposure is on, a note that no backup group was found.
Otherwise it raises the original error, never a fallback's, with outcome text when exposure is on.
Step stop (Immediate stop): Disabled fallbacks, a missing group name, a guardrail block, or a bad request the operator does not let fall back ends the request here.
Step order (Order levels): This path runs only for groups with two or more priority tiers, and not for too-long prompts or blocked content.
Step wf (Weighted failover): This path runs only when the operator turned it on and the group shuffles by weight.
Step ded (Dedicated lists): Too-long prompts and blocked content use their own backup lists alone when set, never the general list; otherwise they use the general list.
note: RDISP-108: "A `ContextWindowExceededError` with `context_window_fallbacks` not `None` is decided by that list alone; the generic `fallbacks` chain is never consulted for it" (RDISP-110 the same for content policy); RDISP-109, now cited: with the list `None` the error "continues to the generic chain". "Never" is now tied to "when set". (A non-standard `fallbacks` value is checked before the dedicated lists, per RDISP-107 and IF-147, but this step, like RDISP-108, is about the generic chain.)

sentence: Step gen (General list): An entry for the group itself wins over the catch-all entry.
Step walk>orig (Every backup fails): The caller gets the original error, not a backup's, with a note on what was tried when the operator allows it.
After each provider call, the router's logging callbacks update its counters, except for calls without router bookkeeping.
A success adds to the deployment's counts, and a failure can bench the deployment for a few seconds.
For a counted success, `deployment_callback_on_success` adds 1 to the in-memory `<id>:successes` key for 60 s.
It adds per-minute token and request usage only for deployments with limits, minus what the loop already counted at response time.
It swallows its own errors and skips realtime sessions and batch retrieves.

On failure, `deployment_callback_on_failure` skips advisor-orchestration errors, provider 404s from background-response polls, 408s from a caller-set timeout and caller-scoped authentication failures.
Otherwise it takes a `cooldown_time` from the deployment, then the error's `retry-after`, then the router, 5 s by default.
With a deployment id, it adds 1 to `<id>:fails`, asks the cooldown handler whether to bench the deployment, and re-raises its own errors.
Without a configured id, `generate_model_id` hashes the group name and each setting's key and value in insertion order with SHA-256, so reordering settings changes the id.
Embeddings, file uploads and batch jobs have their own entry points.
An upload goes to every healthy deployment at once; a batch lookup asks many at once and returns the first match.
Embeddings run through the same fallback entry.
`acreate_file` returns the first upload's response with a map from deployment id to file id.
It never falls back to another group, and a retry re-uploads everywhere.
If one upload fails, that error surfaces while the others keep running.
`acreate_batch` and `acancel_batch` each select one deployment and run through the fallback entry, so a retried create can make a second batch.
`aretrieve_batch` asks every healthy deployment, or every router deployment without a model, and returns the first batch found, without retries.
Several endpoint names, including some video, interaction and container-file calls, return nothing without calling the provider, so the caller gets an empty result and no error.
A request that runs out of retries still waits one more pause before any backup starts, delaying its reply or error.
A request that asks for zero retries gets none, even when a retry policy would retry its error; a router-wide zero does not override a policy.

A retry policy that covers bad requests (status 400) retries them, though the eligibility check would normally stop them. Every retry re-sends the whole job, so a retried batch creation can make a second batch.
A dedicated backup list for too-long prompts or blocked content overrides the general list: with no matching entry, not even a catch-all, the request fails at once.
When an order-level walk fails, the caller gets that walk's last error instead of the original, with no explanation.
A file upload to several deployments that fails part-way can leave files behind that the reply's file map does not list and nothing removes.
A caller who can pass internal settings can raise its own backup limit.
